terms.title: Albedo
terms.summary: Albedo is essentially another word for Base color. Base Color/Albedo is a map without lighting, shadow, or highlights.

terms.title: Base Color
terms.summary: Basecolor is essentially another word for Albedo. Base Color/Albedo is a map without lighting, shadow, or highlights.

terms.title: Beveling
terms.summary: Beveling (also called chamfering) is the process of rounding or flattening the edge of a 3D model. This helps surfaces catch highlights, improves realism, and is critical for producing clean high-poly models for baking.

terms.title: ZBrush
terms.summary: ZBrush is a digital sculpting application used to create highly detailed models. Artists can work with millions of polygons, making it ideal for organic forms, characters, and high-resolution detail work in games and film.

terms.title: Smooth Mesh Preview
terms.summary: Smooth Mesh Preview in Maya allows artists to preview a subdivided (smoothed) version of their model without permanently applying subdivision. It is used to visualize how a low-poly cage will look when smoothed.

terms.title: Dynamesh
terms.summary: Dynamesh is a ZBrush feature that redistributes topology evenly across a mesh while sculpting. It behaves like a voxel-based system, allowing shapes to merge and change freely without stretched polygons, but does not maintain clean, animation-ready topology.

terms.title: Remeshing
terms.summary: Remeshing regenerates the topology of a mesh, but behaves very differently depending on the software. In ZBrush, Remesh tools (like ZRemesher) produce clean, all-quad topology with even edge flow ideal for sculpting. In Maya, the Remesh tool behaves more like a voxelizer, producing a triangulated mesh similar to Dynamesh, which is NOT ideal for sculpting or animation. Because of this, Maya users typically use the Retopologize tool instead when they need clean, quad-based topology.

terms.title: Retopology
terms.summary: Retopology is the process of rebuilding a mesh with clean, efficient topology. In Maya, the Retopologize tool is used to create evenly distributed, quad-based geometry suitable for animation and production. Unlike Maya’s Remesh (which creates triangulated, voxel-like output), Retopologize produces structured edge flow similar to ZBrush’s ZRemesher, making it the preferred tool for creating production-ready meshes.

terms.title: 12 Principles of Animation
terms.summary: The 12 Principles of Animation are foundational guidelines created by Disney animators. They include Squash and Stretch, Anticipation, Staging, Straight Ahead vs Pose-to-Pose, Follow Through and Overlapping Action, Slow In and Slow Out, Arcs, Secondary Action, Timing, Exaggeration, Solid Drawing, and Appeal. These principles help create believable movement and performance.

terms.title: Light Mapping
terms.summary: Light mapping is the process of baking lighting and shadow information into textures that are applied to static objects. It allows realistic lighting while keeping real-time performance costs low.

terms.title: LOD
terms.summary: Level of Detail (LOD) refers to multiple versions of an asset with decreasing complexity at different distances. This can include reduced geometry, simpler materials, or disabling lights to improve performance.

terms.title: Draw Calls
terms.summary: Draw calls are instructions sent from the CPU to the GPU to render objects. Each mesh, material slot, or actor increases draw calls. High draw call counts negatively impact performance, especially in Unreal Engine and indie projects where optimization is critical.

terms.title: Nanite
terms.summary: Nanite is Unreal Engine 5’s virtualized geometry system that allows extremely high-polygon models to render in real time by dynamically streaming only visible detail.

terms.title: Lumen
terms.summary: Lumen is Unreal Engine 5’s real-time global illumination system that simulates light bouncing and reflections dynamically without requiring baked lighting.

terms.title: Global Illumination
terms.summary: Global Illumination simulates how light bounces between surfaces, affecting color and brightness. Real-time solutions include Unreal’s Lumen, while offline renderers like Arnold and Cycles produce higher-quality but slower results.

terms.title: Bounce Light
terms.summary: Bounce light is indirect light that reflects off surfaces and illuminates other parts of a scene, contributing to realistic shading and color bleeding.

terms.title: 3-Point Lighting
terms.summary: Three-point lighting uses a key light, fill light, and back light to illuminate a subject clearly while maintaining depth and contrast.

terms.title: Key Light
terms.summary: The key light is the main light source in a scene, defining the overall lighting direction and strongest shadows.

terms.title: Fill Light
terms.summary: The fill light softens and reduces shadows created by the key light, helping control contrast.

terms.title: High Key vs Low Key
terms.summary: High-key lighting uses bright, even illumination with minimal shadows, while low-key lighting emphasizes contrast and deep shadows for dramatic effect.

terms.title: Exposure
terms.summary: Exposure determines how bright or dark an image appears based on light intensity and camera settings. In Unreal Engine, exposure can be controlled dynamically through post-process volumes.

terms.title: Post Process
terms.summary: Post-processing includes visual effects applied after rendering, such as color grading, bloom, depth of field, and exposure adjustments.

terms.title: Gestalt
terms.summary: Gestalt principles describe how humans perceive visual elements as unified wholes rather than separate pieces, influencing composition and design.

terms.title: Environment Artist
terms.summary: An Environment Artist builds full game worlds, combining modeling, texturing, lighting, and composition. This role goes beyond just modeling assets.

terms.title: Gameplay Animator
terms.summary: A Gameplay Animator creates animations that respond to player input and gameplay systems, unlike cinematic animators who focus on pre-scripted scenes.

terms.title: JIRA
terms.summary: JIRA is a project management tool used in game development to track tasks, bugs, and production progress.

terms.title: Perforce
terms.summary: Perforce is a version control system widely used in game development for managing large files and team collaboration.

terms.title: Version Control
terms.summary: Version control systems track changes to files over time, allowing teams to collaborate and revert to previous versions. Examples include Git, Perforce, and SVN.

terms.title: Motivated vs Unmotivated Lighting
terms.summary: Motivated lighting comes from a believable source within the scene, like a lamp, window, or fire, helping the viewer understand where the light originates. Unmotivated lighting has no visible or logical source and is used stylistically to highlight subjects or improve readability. Strong lighting design often blends both approaches.

terms.title: Area / Rect Lights
terms.summary: Area (Rect) lights simulate large light sources and produce softer, more realistic shadows and reflections. In Unreal Engine 5, they are more expensive than point or directional lights because they calculate surface area, soft shadow falloff, and reflections, so overuse can negatively impact performance.

terms.title: PlayerStart Actor
terms.summary: The PlayerStart Actor defines where the player spawns when the level begins. It determines the player's starting position and orientation in the game world.

terms.title: Actor
terms.summary: An Actor is any object that exists in a level in Unreal Engine, including meshes, lights, cameras, and gameplay elements. Actors can contain components and logic that define their behavior.

terms.title: Control Rig
terms.summary: Control Rig allows animators to create rigs and animate characters directly inside Unreal Engine 5. It provides controls for posing, procedural animation, and editing without leaving the engine.

terms.title: Level Sequence
terms.summary: A Level Sequence is Unreal Engine’s cinematic timeline system used to animate cameras, actors, lights, and events over time. It works similarly to animation timelines in film or video editing software.

terms.title: Aperture
terms.summary: Aperture is the opening of a camera lens that controls how much light enters. A wider aperture (low f-stop) lets in more light and creates shallow depth of field, while a smaller aperture (high f-stop) results in a darker image with more of the scene in focus. Unreal’s cinematic cameras simulate this behavior.

terms.title: F-Stops
terms.summary: F-stops measure the size of a lens opening. Lower values (like f/1.8) mean more light and blurrier backgrounds, while higher values (like f/16) mean less light and sharper images. In Unreal Engine, f-stops affect both exposure and depth of field behavior.

terms.title: FOV vs Focal Length
terms.summary: Field of View (FOV) controls how wide the camera sees and is commonly used in gameplay cameras. Focal length controls lens behavior and is used in cinematic cameras. Wide FOV exaggerates perspective, while long focal lengths compress depth and feel more realistic.

terms.title: Focal Length
terms.summary: Focal length defines how a camera lens represents perspective. Short focal lengths (wide lenses) exaggerate space, while long focal lengths (telephoto lenses) compress depth. In Unreal and Maya, cinematic cameras rely on focal length instead of FOV for physically accurate results.

terms.title: Golden Ratio
terms.summary: The Golden Ratio (approximately 1.618) is a mathematical proportion used to create visually pleasing compositions. It is often visualized as a spiral guiding the viewer’s eye through an image.

terms.title: Phi Grid
terms.summary: The Phi Grid is based on the Golden Ratio and divides an image into sections that create more natural balance than the Rule of Thirds. It is used to place focal points more precisely.

terms.title: Rule of Thirds
terms.summary: The Rule of Thirds divides an image into a 3x3 grid. Placing important elements along the lines or intersections creates more engaging and balanced compositions.

terms.title: Principles of Design
terms.summary: The principles of design include balance, contrast, emphasis, movement, rhythm, unity, and variety. These concepts help organize visual elements to create clear, effective compositions.

terms.title: Line Quality
terms.summary: Line quality refers to the variation in thickness, darkness, and flow of lines. Strong line work uses variation to show depth, emphasize form, and guide the viewer’s eye.

terms.title: Edge Quality & Control
terms.summary: Edge quality describes how sharp or soft transitions are between forms. Artists use hard, soft, and lost edges to control focus. In sculpting, edge control defines form clarity and surface quality.

terms.title: Depth of Field
terms.summary: Depth of field determines how much of a scene is in focus. Shallow depth of field blurs the background to emphasize a subject. In Unreal Engine, this is controlled using aperture (low f-stop), focus distance, and cinematic camera or post-process settings.

terms.title: Monochromatic
terms.summary: A monochromatic color scheme uses variations of a single color, including tints (lighter), shades (darker), and tones (muted). This creates a cohesive and controlled look, often emphasizing value and form over color complexity.

terms.title: Complementary
terms.summary: Complementary colors are opposite each other on the color wheel (like blue and orange). When used together, they create strong contrast and visual energy, making subjects stand out.

terms.title: Analogous
terms.summary: Analogous colors sit next to each other on the color wheel (like blue, blue-green, and green). These schemes feel harmonious and natural because the colors are closely related.

terms.title: Analogous with Complementary Accent
terms.summary: This scheme uses an analogous palette for harmony but adds a small amount of a complementary color for contrast. This allows an image to feel unified while still having a strong focal point.

terms.title: Split Complementary
terms.summary: A split complementary scheme uses one base color and the two colors adjacent to its complement. It maintains strong contrast like complementary colors but is less intense and easier to balance.

terms.title: Color Wheel
terms.summary: The color wheel organizes colors and shows relationships like complementary and analogous schemes. In additive color (light, like screens), colors combine toward white (RGB). In subtractive color (paint/pigment), colors combine toward black or muddy tones (RYB/CMY). One important thing for artists to understand is that complementary colors are NOT always the same depending on which color system you are using. Traditional painting (RYB) uses pairs like red/green or blue/orange, while digital and lighting workflows (RGB) shift those relationships. Because of this, what counts as a 'true complement' can change depending on whether you’re working in paint, Photoshop, or Unreal Engine, so always consider your medium.

terms.title: Color Temperature
terms.summary: Color temperature describes whether a color feels warm (reds, oranges) or cool (blues). In lighting, it is measured in Kelvin. Lower Kelvin values (like 2000K) produce warm light like fire, mid values (5000–6500K) resemble daylight, and higher values create cool, blue light. In Unreal and digital art, using Kelvin values can quickly achieve realistic lighting, such as warm campfires, glowing heated metal (which shifts from red to white as it heats), or neutral daylight.

terms.title: Inverse Square Law
terms.summary: The inverse square law states that light intensity decreases rapidly as distance increases. If you double the distance from a light, it becomes one-fourth as bright. Unreal Engine’s physically based lighting follows this rule, making correct light placement and scale critical for realism.

terms.title: Collision
terms.summary: Collision defines how objects physically interact in a game world. It determines where players can walk, what blocks movement, and how objects behave. Environment artists must create clean, optimized collision to ensure gameplay works correctly without hurting performance.

terms.title: Normals
terms.summary: Normals are vectors that tell a surface which direction it is facing, which is critical for how light interacts with that surface. Even simple geometry can appear smooth or faceted depending on how its normals are configured.

terms.title: Vertex Normals
terms.summary: Vertex normals define shading at each vertex and are averaged between faces to create smooth shading. When vertex normals are shared between faces, the surface appears smooth. When they are split, the surface appears hard or faceted. This is often referred to as soft vs hard edges.

terms.title: Face Normals
terms.summary: Face normals represent the direction of an individual polygon. When shading uses face normals instead of shared vertex normals, the object appears faceted, with visible polygon edges.

terms.title: Hard vs Soft Edges
terms.summary: Hard edges split vertex normals between faces, creating sharp transitions (faceted shading). Soft edges share vertex normals, smoothing the shading between faces. These do not change geometry—only how lighting is calculated.

terms.title: Face Weighted Normals
terms.summary: Face weighted normals adjust vertex normals so larger faces have more influence over shading. This helps hard surface models appear smoother and cleaner without adding extra geometry, making it especially useful in game art workflows.

terms.title: Smooth Shading vs Subdivision
terms.summary: A major point of confusion is that 'smoothing' can mean different things. In most 3D apps, smoothing refers to vertex normals being averaged to create smooth shading. In Maya, however, 'Smooth' often means subdividing geometry (adding more polygons). These are not the same—one changes shading, the other changes geometry.

terms.title: Texel Density
terms.summary: Texel density refers to how much texture resolution is applied across a surface. Consistent texel density ensures that all parts of an asset have similar visual sharpness, preventing some areas from looking blurry while others are overly detailed.

terms.title: World Aligned Texture
terms.summary: A world aligned texture applies a material based on world coordinates instead of UVs. This makes textures automatically align across multiple objects and is useful for environment work like terrain, cliffs, and large surfaces.

terms.title: Decals
terms.summary: Decals are projected textures used to add localized detail like dirt, damage, signs, or graffiti without modifying the base material. In Unreal, deferred decals allow detail layering while keeping assets modular and efficient.

terms.title: Shader Complexity
terms.summary: Shader complexity refers to how expensive a material is to render. More complex shaders require more GPU processing. Unreal Engine provides visualization modes to help artists identify and optimize costly materials.

terms.title: Lightmass vs Lumen
terms.summary: Lightmass is Unreal’s baked lighting system, where light is precomputed into lightmaps for performance. Lumen is Unreal Engine 5’s real-time global illumination system, dynamically calculating light bounces. Lightmass is more performance-friendly, while Lumen is more flexible and realistic in dynamic scenes.

terms.title: Root Motion
terms.summary: Root motion refers to animation where the character’s movement is driven by the animation itself (like walking forward). Instead of the game moving the character, the animation controls translation, which can increase realism but requires careful setup.

terms.title: In-Place Animation
terms.summary: In-place animation keeps the character moving in place (like running on a treadmill), while the game engine handles movement. This is common in games because it allows better control over speed and navigation.

terms.title: Animation Blueprint
terms.summary: An Animation Blueprint in Unreal Engine controls how animations play and blend based on gameplay logic. It allows developers to connect animations to player input, states, and transitions.

terms.title: State Machine
terms.summary: A state machine controls transitions between animations (such as idle, walk, run, jump). It defines rules for switching between states based on conditions like speed or player input.

terms.title: Blend Space
terms.summary: A blend space allows multiple animations to smoothly blend together based on input values like speed or direction. For example, blending between idle, walk, and run animations based on movement speed.

terms.title: Pivot / Origin
terms.summary: The pivot (or origin point) is the center point from which an object moves, rotates, and scales. Proper pivot placement is essential for animation, snapping objects together, and correct behavior in game engines.

terms.title: Scale
terms.summary: Scale refers to the size of objects in relation to real-world measurements. Maintaining correct scale is critical in Unreal Engine for physics, lighting, and player interaction to feel believable.

terms.title: Naming Conventions
terms.summary: Naming conventions are standardized ways of naming files, assets, and objects. Consistent naming helps teams stay organized, improves communication, and prevents errors in large projects.

terms.title: Optimization Budget
terms.summary: An optimization budget defines limits for things like triangle count, draw calls, and texture resolution. Artists must work within these limits to ensure the game runs smoothly while maintaining visual quality.

terms.title: Overdraw
terms.summary: Overdraw occurs when multiple transparent or layered pixels are rendered on top of each other, causing the GPU to repeatedly draw the same screen space. This commonly happens with foliage, particles, decals, and translucent materials. High overdraw is expensive because the GPU must process each layer even if it's hidden behind another. In Unreal Engine, overdraw is often visualized in debug views, and reducing it (by simplifying materials, limiting transparency, or adjusting mesh density) is critical for performance.

terms.title: Instruction Count
terms.summary: Instruction count refers to how many operations a shader performs to calculate the final pixel color. More instructions mean a more expensive material. Complex node setups, layered materials, and excessive math increase instruction count and reduce performance. In Unreal Engine’s Material Editor, instruction count is displayed to help artists optimize shaders and keep them within real-time performance budgets.
